description: We are a multidisciplinary team with backgrounds in Software Engineering, Data Analytics, and Cybersecurity, passionate about innovation and space exploration. Our goal is to develop an intuitive, data-driven Lunar Landing Site Navigator. We bring skills in software development, data analysis, and problem-solving. We're looking for creative teammates interested in astronomy, space science, UI/UX, and data visualization. Join us to explore the Moon together!
summary:
Artemis Atlas is an interactive web application designed to help users identify and compare optimal lunar landing conditions at the Moon’s South Pole. By selecting a location on a 3D lunar globe and choosing a date, users can explore how the positions of the Sun and Earth affect solar energy availability and direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication.

Powered by NASA SPICE ephemerides, Artemis Atlas calculates solar elevation and azimuth, visible solar disk percentage, time until sunrise or sunset, total sunlight hours, and Earth elevation and visibility. It also simulates the complete 29.5-day lunar cycle and enables side-by-side comparison of up to three landing scenarios.

With Basic and Advanced modes, the application makes complex orbital geometry accessible to both mission planners and the general public. By bringing essential mission-planning insights into a single interactive platform, Artemis Atlas aims to identify potential power and communication risks earlier, supporting safer and more informed lunar exploration.
details:
What it does and how it works
Artemis Atlas is a web app for comparing lunar south pole landing sites and dates. The user clicks any point on an interactive 3D Moon globe (or uses quick shortcuts like “South Pole”) and picks a date. The app computes the geometry between the Sun, Earth and that point from NASA SPICE ephemerides, and shows:

  • Solar elevation and azimuth, and the percentage of the solar disk above the horizon.
  • Time until sunset or sunrise, and total hours of sunlight in the lunar-day window.
  • Earth elevation and visibility, which is the requirement for direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication.
  • A simulation of the full 29.5-day lunar cycle.
  • A side-by-side comparison of up to three site-and-date scenarios.

It has two modes. Basic answers the essentials at a glance: past landing sites, available solar energy, Earth signal and remaining daylight. Advanced shows elevation, azimuth, libration and scenario comparison.

Benefits and intended impact
Today, answering “will this site have power and a link to Earth on this date?” requires chaining specialist tools (SPICE, terrain models, STK, spreadsheets). We give that answer in seconds, in a browser, to mission planners, educators and the public. The aim is to catch energy and communication risks early in mission planning, like the conditions that ended Athena’s mission in 2025 after under 13 hours, and to make lunar exploration easier to understand for everyone.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA SPICE ephemerides (NAIF). LOLA topography is planned for real-horizon profiles.
  • Front-end: HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Three.js for the 3D globe.
  • Back-end / calculations: Python + SpiceyPy, or a JS port.
  • Other: hosting, design tools, AI tools used for images or video.

Creativity
Instead of another layered map viewer, we show the sky from the landing site’s point of view: where the Sun and Earth sit over the local horizon, and how that changes over time. The Basic/Advanced split means the same tool works for a classroom and an engineering team.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: we separate measured data, predictions and derived values. The current version uses a geometric horizon (no terrain), which we state openly; LOLA terrain is the next step.
  • Usability: answers in seconds, with minimal jargon in Basic mode.
  • Open data: reproducible, traceable NASA sources.
  • Scalability: the architecture can add terrain, thermal data (Diviner) and communications models in future versions.
